FILLED UP.—The swampy tract of land lying between Maryland avenue and the Wilmington & Reading Railroad, is being filled up, and a cart way made from the avenue to the coal bins of the Company.

SABBATH SCHOOL DEMONSTRATION.—Delegates from the various Sabbath Schools will meet at the Central Presbyterian Church tomorrow evening, at eight o'clock, to take further action in the Grand Children's Demonstration.

NEEDS ATTENTION. The condition of King street, between Eighth and Ninth, about twenty cart loads of dirt have been heaped up by the street cleaners and left to be scattered again by passing teams. It should be removed without delay.

NOMINATION.—At meeting of the citizens of the Third Ward, representatives of party, held last evening, at the Commercial office, Mr. Solomon Hersey was nominated for member of the Board of Education. The vote stood: Hersey, 80; John Peoples, 9.

PRIMITIVE STYLE OF ADVERTISING.—An enterprising individual in the western part of the city advertises for boarders by posting written notice upon a tree. Let him advertise in the DAILY GAZETTE, and we will insure him an abundance of boarders.

IMPROVED.—The crossings at the Junction of Monroe and Chestnut streets and Maryland avenue, which have been in an almost impossible condition for some time, are being cleaned and the beds of the streets filled. Plates are also being placed over the cutters.

SLIGHT FIRE.—The alarm of fire about half past three o'clock yesterday afternoon, was occasioned by the burning of a pot of composition, in the building at Ninth and Church streets; recently occupied by Maury James, as a match factory. No material damage was sustained.

A New STAR.—Miss Cassie HEM, the celebrated cantatrice, of New York, whose voice, it is said rivals even Nilsson's in power, has accepted an invitation from a number of gentlemen of this city, and will give a concert in the Masonic Temple, on the evening of April 23d.

POLICE CASES. Four cases of drunkenness were disposed of by the Mayor this morning. Fifty cents and costs in each case. Henry Brown, colored, was arrested for drunkenness and attempting to break into the house of Henry Carpenter. Fined $1 and costs.

The New LODGE ROOMS. The new lodge rooms in the new Masonic Temple are rapidly approaching completion. Every adornment consistent with neatness and good taste will be placed therein, and in appearance they will far exceed any society rooms in this city. The rooms will be finished in time for the dedication of the Temple, which takes place on the 18th of this month. To Mr. R. A. GILPIN, the Architect, is due the credit of the drawings from which the new temple is designed. Mr. Gilpin is a practical civil engineer and architect and all his work is done with remarkable precision, skill and neatness. The Messrs. Gilbert it would seem, will have nearly as much room for practical use in each of the new stores that there was in the old.

CAPY Town GOATS.—Messrs. Pusey, Scott & Co., have about fifteen goats, of various sizes, in the yard of their morocco factory, Third and Madison streets, which were imported from Capetown, Africa. They are greatly similar to native goats in appearance, but are of rather brisk and vicious temperament. Several of the animals are to be sent to Virginia, with the view of propagating the species.

MUTUAL AID SOCIETY.—A meeting composed of members from the various lodges of Knights of Pythias, of this city, was held last evening in their hall, in Morrow's building, for the purpose of forming "Knights of Pythias Mutual Aid Society." The following officers were elected: President, Peyton S. West; Vice President, Edwin Hirst; Secretary, Samuel Curry; Treasurer, A. R. Hollingsworth. A committee, consisting of three members, was appointed to prepare Constitution and bylaws, and the meeting adjourned to meet again at the call of this committee.

FREIGHT TRAINS.—The heavy shipments of coal over the W. Il. R. R. still continue. At the W. Il. R. R. freight depot, the following have been received since last report from Philadelphia: one of wheat, one of bone, one of hogs, two of stone, one of machinery, and two of coal.

The success which attended the first public concert of the Nashville Choral Society, when they performed Handel's grand oratorio, "The Messiah" to one of the largest audiences ever attracted to an amateur entertainment in Nashville, induced the Society to repeat it last night. They were influenced to do so by the urgent solicitations of host of friends who had heard their first entertainment, and by as many who were unable to attend on that occasion and were anxious to hear Handel's great masterpiece. Masonic Hall was secured for last night, and due notice of the Concert was given. In the meantime the Society, numbering some fifty singers, practiced the oratorio with great assiduity, determined, if possible, to eclipse their former effort. To prepare for the occasion, much time, great pains and considerable sum of money was expended. It was somewhat disheartening, therefore, to find about one third of the seats in the hall unoccupied last night. True the audience was much larger than many first class entertainments have been able to call together in Nashville, and it comprised the elite of the city, but a concert combining the best amateur talent in the city should have filled Masonic Hall till standing room could not be found. As it is, the receipts will about cover the heavy expenditures, and no more.

The concert was opened at half past 1 o'clock, 18th by a brilliant overture by the Society and an excellent orchestra. The choruses throughout the oratorio were rendered with fine effect, and without a discordant or faulty note to mar the harmony. The time was simply perfect, every voice and every instrument pursuing the difficult strains as if controlled by the volition of single person. Nothing but long and patient practice under skillful direction could have produced such admirable symphony.

The solos were all well rendered—some with remarkable power and brilliancy. Among the ladies, Mrs. Ida Rains, Mrs. French and Mrs. H. Vessel seemed to be the favorites with the audience. Miss Cotton, Miss H. Hasslock and Mrs. Beauman sang their solos with much sweetness and expression. Mrs. Ida Rains and Mrs. French possess exceedingly fine and well cultivated voices. Their solos (they sang but one each) were among the most brilliant gems in the entertainment of the evening. Mrs. H. Vessel received an enthusiastic encore to her rendering of the air "I know that my Redeemer liveth." In return she favored the audience with polite courtesy—"only this and nothing more."

Among the gentlemen, Messrs. Jackson, J. Ashford and Molengraft, and James Anderson, sang solo. The only one rendered by Mr. Jackson, "Why do the Nations So furiously rage together" was enthusiastically encored, but he declined to respond to the call. The other gentlemen sang their parts most creditably, and the audience testified their appreciation by frequent applause.

A quartet by Miss Cotton, Mrs. Vessel, Mr. Molengraft and Mr. Jackson, with chorus by the entire society was fully rendered.

The oratorio was on the whole one of the most successful entertainments of the kind ever given by amateurs in Nashville, surpassing in all but the size of the audience even the former concert of the society.

"A leech? Not a bee?"

an adept in the art to decipher the express-

hunted look which told of great suffering,
either mental or physical—probably the
former, for the deep lines about his mouth
and eyes were of that character which is

a terrible, because secret, sorrow. I
cannot say that you would have gathered all

feminine adornment which fathers and
husbands pay so highly for.
